note: TCP itself never times out an idle connection, but load balancers, NATs and firewalls on the path do, so long-lived connections need keep-alives or periodic data.
checker_note: True at the protocol level: TCP has no idle timeout, keep-alives are optional, off by default and at least 2 hours apart (RFC 9293). In practice, middleboxes on the path close idle connections: load balancers (AWS ALB idle timeout defaults to 60 s), NATs and firewalls. A learner designing an hour-long request must send data or keep-alives, or raise those timeouts; otherwise the connection is dropped silently.

additions.text: AWS Application Load Balancers close a connection that has been idle (no data in either direction) for the idle timeout, 60 seconds by default and configurable from 1 to 4000 seconds. For long operations, AWS advises sending at least 1 byte before each idle period ends and setting the application's own idle timeout above the load balancer's.

TCP keep-alives are optional in the TCP standard; if implemented they must be off by default, and the interval must default to no less than two hours (RFC 9293). So unless the application sends data or its own heartbeats, an idle TCP connection may not notice for hours that the peer is gone.

note: HTTP/1.0 closed the connection after each response unless keep-alive was used; HTTP/1.1 keeps connections open by default.
checker_note: Reversed default: since HTTP/1.1, connections are persistent by default, and a client or server must send 'Connection: close' to end one. Closing after each response was HTTP/1.0 behaviour, where the 'keep-alive' option kept the connection open. Persistence also does not by itself let one request run for an hour; idle timeouts on proxies still apply.

additions.text: HTTP/1.1 uses persistent connections by default: several requests and responses share one connection until someone sends 'Connection: close'. Under HTTP/1.0 the connection stayed open only if the 'keep-alive' option was sent and honored (RFC 9112, section 9.3).

note: gRPC does use long-lived HTTP/2 connections that the protocol does not time out (server MAX_CONNECTION_IDLE and MAX_CONNECTION_AGE default to infinite).
